card.title: Limits — what a function approaches, not what it equals

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) gets arbitrarily close to L as x closes in on a — from either side, and crucially without ever requiring x = a. The point itself may be undefined and the limit still exist, which is why (x²−4)/(x−2), undefined at 2, still has limit 4. A speedometer shows a limit: average velocity over a shrinking interval.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: ε–δ: |f(x)−L|<ε whenever 0<|x−a|<δ (the 0< excludes the point itself)  ·  two-sided exists ⟺ lim(x→a⁻) = lim(x→a⁺) = L, finite  ·  standard: lim(x→0) sinx/x = 1 (radians only)  ·  signals, not answers: 0/0, ∞/∞, ∞−∞, 0·∞, 1^∞, 0^0, ∞^0

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Always substitute first; rewrite only when substitution fails with an indeterminate form. The two-sided limit demands both one-sided limits exist AND agree — equal-but-different, or −∞/+∞ splits, mean no limit. Infinity is shorthand for unbounded growth, never a value.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: A jump discontinuity kills the two-sided limit (left ≠ right). Opposite-sign one-sided infinities mark a vertical asymptote; a finite limit at infinity marks a horizontal one (dominant-term rule). A 0/0 hole like (x²−4)/(x−2) is removable — factor, cancel, then substitute.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: lim(x→4) (x²−16)/(x−4): direct substitution gives 0/0, so factorise → (x−4)(x+4)/(x−4). Near (not at) x = 4 the factor cancels, leaving lim(x→4) (x+4) = 8. Contrast lim(x→5) (x−2)/(x−5): no 0/0, but the point itself is undefined — one-sided infinities, vertical asymptote, no limit.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Writing 'lim = ∞' as a result is wrong — divergence reports unboundedness, not a value. A limit is not continuity: continuity additionally needs f(a) defined and equal to the limit. sinx/x = 1 holds in radians only; in degrees the limit is π/180.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Why cancelling is legal: 0<|x−4| in the ε–δ definition excludes x = 4 itself, so (x−4)/(x−4) = 1 everywhere the limit examines, and (x²−16)/(x−4) coincides with x+4 on that punctured neighbourhood. Equal functions on the examined set share the limit — hence 8, rigorously, not by luck.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: 0/0 → factor and cancel; ∞/∞ → divide by the highest power; roots → multiply by the conjugate; trig → force sinx/x. For asymptotes check one-sided signs, not just magnitudes. And the derivative itself is a limit — f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h — so every differentiation rule rests on this card.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: NEB-style (unit practice bank): state the ε–δ definition and explain why 0<|x−a| appears; evaluate lim(x→4)(x²−16)/(x−4) and lim(x→5)(x−2)/(x−5), stating which is undefined at the point; find the horizontal and vertical asymptotes of y = (2x+1)/(x²−4).
